glance.why: London is one of the rare cities where imperial history, royal ceremony, world-class museums, theatre, finance, fashion, immigration and contemporary food culture all coexist within a remarkably walkable central core. The city rewards travelers who alternate major landmarks with neighborhood wandering rather than trying to treat it as a checklist. For a first visit, the strongest combination is Westminster + the Thames + the Tower/City + one or two major museums + a West End evening + several neighborhood meals. London is large enough that 4-5 days feels substantially better than a rushed 2-3 day visit. Research broadly, then curate aggressively: prioritize experiences that explain the city rather than collecting attractions simply because they are famous.
glance.idealStay: 4-5 days; 6-7+ days if adding deeper museums, day trips and outer neighborhoods
dontMiss: South Bank and the Thames walk
A proper pub or food experience

history.story: London makes more sense when understood as several cities layered on top of one another. Roman Londinium grew around a strategic crossing of the Thames. Medieval London developed around the City and the royal seat at Westminster. Tudor and Stuart London expanded the courtly and commercial city; the Great Fire of 1666 forced major rebuilding. The Industrial Revolution turned London into the center of a global empire, while Victorian infrastructure - railways, bridges, sewers and the Underground - created much of the physical city visitors recognize today.
history.origins: The Thames made London valuable: it provided a navigable commercial route inland and a connection to the sea. The Roman settlement occupied the area around today's City of London, where traces of the Roman wall and amphitheatre remain.

food.identity: London's food identity is less about one cuisine than about extraordinary density and diversity. Traditional British food - fish and chips, pies, Sunday roast, full English breakfast and afternoon tea - still matters, but modern London is equally defined by Indian, Middle Eastern, Chinese, Southeast Asian, Caribbean, African, European and contemporary British cooking. The key is to eat both sides of the city: one deliberately traditional meal and several meals in neighborhoods shaped by immigration.

timeGuidance.three: Prioritize Westminster, the Tower and the City, one major museum, South Bank and the Thames, and one West End evening.
timeGuidance.fivePlus: With 4-5 days add Soho and Covent Garden, a second museum, a market or food neighborhood and more relaxed park time. With more than five days, explore Hampstead, Greenwich, Kew, Camden, Notting Hill, deeper museums and a day trip.

practical.gettingAround: Use the Underground, Elizabeth line, Overground, buses and walking as the default. Contactless payment is usually the simplest option for visitors; Oyster remains useful if you do not have a suitable contactless card or device. Always use the same card or device when touching in and out so the system can calculate fares and apply capping. Walking is excellent for linking nearby central sights, but do not underestimate distances between zones. The Tube is fastest for many cross-city journeys, while buses are often better for seeing the city while moving. Taxis and ride-hailing are useful late at night or with luggage, but rarely necessary for ordinary sightseeing. Use Thames river services when the route is genuinely useful rather than treating every boat ride as an attraction.
practical.whenToGo: Spring offers an excellent balance of greenery, daylight and walking weather. Summer has the longest days and fullest event calendar, but higher crowds and prices. Autumn brings a strong museum and theatre season with attractive parks, and is generally a good city-break period. Winter is colder and darker, but excellent for theatre, museums, shopping and festive atmosphere.

howLong.one: Westminster, the Thames, one major landmark and a central dinner or theatre evening.
howLong.twoThree: Enough for the classic first-timer circuit, but still rushed.
howLong.fourFive: The ideal balance of major sights plus neighborhood exploration.
howLong.week: Best for travelers who want museums, food neighborhoods, parks and day trips.

culture: Queueing is expected and generally orderly.
On escalators, stand on the right and walk on the left.
Pub culture is casual; order at the bar unless table service is indicated.
Tipping is not mandatory in the American sense; check whether a service charge is already included.
Londoners generally value personal space and efficient, unobtrusive behavior on public transport.
